Tina quoted the firm's standard terms for corrective work: a corrective drafting fee of about half the original drafting fee, courier and filing costs passed through at cost, and a turnaround of up to two weeks. Fenwick refuses to pay any of it. She points to the one-year window in the engagement terms during which the firm stands behind defective work, and calls the problem an initial flaw in what was filed, so the redraft should be free. Tina asks Jenna Park how to respond.
options: Charge the corrective drafting fee of about half the original fee and pass the courier and filing costs through at cost
Handle the redraft at no charge because the matter falls inside the one-year defective-work window the client cites
Check the firm's standard handling with Arthur Whitfield before replying to the client
invariants: external customer direction kept (the office serves the client)
working-level decision, closed by staff rather than the owner
two participants: the paralegal raising it and the associate advising
corrective-work fee kept at roughly half the original fee, with courier and filing costs passed through separately
turnaround of up to two weeks retained
client's claim rests on the one-year defective-work window in the engagement terms
small, reversible matter settled in a short exchange

situation: A client is reviewing the fee schedule the firm drafted for a batch of small matters. Most line items show a figure produced by applying the standard 1.8x multiplier to the firm's base charge for each item, but a couple of items show a slightly different figure, and the items where no price was applied are still blank. The client asks whether some other pricing basis is used, noting that two items carrying the same base charge differ, and that the first item works out to one figure under the 1.8x rule yet is posted slightly higher — apparently because those figures were made to end in a particular round-looking number. The associate handling the correspondence has to settle how the blank items get filled.
options: Apply a custom price that ends in the round-looking figure the rest of the schedule uses (e.g., a figure ending in 80)
Apply the 1.8x multiplier to the base charge and then round up (e.g., to the next whole figure)
invariants: Working-level pricing call, closed by the associate handling the client's correspondence
Firm sets the price it quotes an external client; the client raises the question but does not decide
The 1.8x multiplier on the base charge remains the default pricing basis
Blank schedule items are filled with the multiplied figure rounded up rather than a hand-picked custom figure
Settled in a short back-and-forth of a few messages

Judge it infeasible and drop it

situation: Our office sends its courthouse filings out through a filing courier, and we are comparing the service tiers that courier offers. Some time ago Mohammed Aziz had gone through the options with the courier and one fuller tier had looked workable. While browsing the courier's other offerings, Tina Russo found a comparable tier at a price she liked better, and she asked in the operations channel whether she should put in a request for a trial run of it, so the office could compare the two tiers before committing to either.
options: Ask the courier for a trial run of the newly found cheaper comparable tier
Go with the tier the office had already discussed with the courier
invariants: Working-level choice, closed by a senior paralegal in the channel where it was raised
Two internal staff involved in the exchange
The firm stays the buyer of an external supplier's service
